Für Kaffee zählt nur der Samen. Haut und: For coffee, only the seed counts. The skin and pulp are removed, and that’s a lot: they make up around 30 per cent of a coffee cherry’s dry mass. With dry processing, about one kilogram of husks is left over for every kilogram of coffee beans.
Ein Teil davon wird zu Dünger oder Tierf: Some of it becomes fertiliser or animal feed. Much of it still ends up in the environment, where it pollutes soil and water. But once dried, the husk has a name of its own: cascara. And you can drink it.
Kaffeekirschen trocknen in der Sonne, fr: Coffee cherries drying in the sun, fresh red ones among dark ones that are already dry
Im Jemen heisst der Aufguss aus Kaffeesc: In Yemen, the infusion made from coffee husks is called Qishr. It’s refined with spices and has been recorded since the 16th century. In Bolivia people drink Sultana, in Ethiopia Hashara. In a tasting study, the panel described cascara infusions as sweetish, fruity and herbal, with notes of honey, prune and black tea.
